turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the twenty-fourth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three headlines. Ukraine says it sank a Russian warship — in a port in Libya.
[excited] Nvidia has taken Jensen Huang back as chief executive, eleven days after he quit, and the shares jumped thirty-one per cent.
And Japan, the country that built a culture on not saying things, has shortlisted the word for saying things as a word of the year.
[laughs] The thread today is "said out loud" — what gets spoken plainly, and what stays half-said.
Let's start in the Mediterranean. At dawn on Sunday the twenty-second, the Russian corvette Merkury was hit at the naval base in Benghazi, in eastern Libya.
[curious] Libya. Not the Black Sea. Libya.
About two thousand kilometres from the Black Sea. It had stopped there for fuel and supplies on its way home. By Sunday it had capsized beside the quay.
And we know that how?
Satellite pictures from Vantor show it moored on Saturday and, on Sunday, "capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible". That's our cover this morning.
[thoughtful] It's an eerie picture. A grey quay, a scorch mark, and a ship lying on its side like a dropped toy.
On Monday Zelensky claimed it. Quote: "Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk."
Seven sea drones, he said. Which are — for anyone wondering — basically small uncrewed boats packed with explosives.
Libyan National Army officials told AP four were shot down and two hit. The casualties are unclear. Reuters' medical sources say ten people slightly hurt. No death toll confirmed.
And the same weekend there's a Russian freighter hit in the Gulf of Finland?
The Sparta Two, bound for Kaliningrad, on the twenty-first. Finland's forces think Ukraine did that too. Kyiv hasn't said.
So how did the capitals read it? Because we've got four on the page.
Moscow first. Dmitry Peskov called it a "dangerous trend" with "very painful consequences for the Kyiv regime". On Libya specifically, just: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements."
[wry] Which is diplomatic for "we're furious and we haven't decided what to say yet".
Beijing's Xinhua datelined it from Tripoli and led with the Libyans — a Presidential Council deputy holding Ukraine "fully responsible" and asking for an emergency Security Council meeting.
Al Jazeera framed it as a war "widening geographically". And the BBC's Frank Gardner asked the obvious question — "where does this stop?"
Now the sceptic. Jalel Harchaoui of RUSI says Khalifa Haftar, who runs eastern Libya, "will take the attack as a personal slight".
Ah. So the operation might cost Ukraine in Libya, even if it worked at sea.
His words: "They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians." And nobody has confirmed where the drones were launched from.
Page four is the other side of the world — India and Nepal.
India promised Nepal nearly one point six billion dollars on Monday, when Narendra Modi received Nepal's prime minister, Balen Shah, in New Delhi.
Balen Shah being the thirty-six-year-old former rapper who became mayor of Kathmandu and then prime minister after last year's youth protests.
That one. But here's the catch. Most of it is a line of credit — a loan to be spent on projects India approves. About four hundred million is grants.
[skeptical] And the Kathmandu Post has seen this movie before.
Their line: "Past announcements of Indian assistance have too often ended with only the grant component reaching Nepal."
And the disputed Lipulekh pass — not raised. Gurkha recruitment — not raised. The paper's verdict: "instruction rather than agreement".
Home, now. Singapore and China signed twenty-nine agreements on Monday at the Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation.
Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong and Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang. Last year was twenty-seven, which was a record, so this is a new high.

The concrete ones are money and food. The Monetary Authority joins the People's Bank of China's yuan repo facility. And Hainan becomes the first Chinese province cleared to send us chilled poultry and shell eggs.
[amused] So the eggs arrive before the payments link.
Exactly that. The fast-payments link, and using Chinese government bonds as collateral — both are things to "explore".
Our sceptic box makes that point without a named critic — we couldn't find one. Just read the list.

A record count of documents is not a record of change. Also on that page: core inflation fell to one point five per cent in October. And the property tax rebate shrinks next year — capped at a hundred dollars, down from five hundred.
And the Prime Minister landed on the first SIA flight into Western Sydney. The leaders' meeting in Canberra is today.
Right. Money. Theo, Monday was a big day.
[laughs] Monday was absurd. The S and P five hundred up four point seven three per cent, Nvidia up thirty-one and a half, the Nasdaq six and a half.
All because Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang before the open. The VIX — the fear gauge — fell from thirty-five point nine on Friday, its highest in a year, to twenty-seven.
Nomura's Charlie McElligott called it a "mechanical bounce" that "guarantees us nothing".
And the regime stands. Futures put a December rate rise at ninety-six per cent. The ten-year real yield closed at two point seven nine.
What was actually new in the data?
A slowdown. S and P Global's flash survey of American business fell to fifty-four point six — a four-month low.
[pause] Okay. The Four. VWRA first.

VWRA's last published NAV was one hundred and seventy-two dollars ninety-seven, Friday's close. Monday's wasn't out at press time. The lean: firmer. A NAV back under that number on the first of December proves it wrong.
PIMCO Income?

The Singapore-dollar hedged class up nought point five eight per cent on the week; the US-dollar class nought point five six. Yields six point eight six and six point five seven. The hedged class lags because hedging costs the gap between American and Singapore short rates.
Gold rose two point seven per cent to about three thousand six hundred and thirty-five dollars. Still twelve per cent under October.
Lean: capped while real yields sit near two point eight. A close above three thousand seven hundred proves it wrong.
And bitcoin — sixty-one thousand three hundred and fourteen dollars at nine in the evening UTC, after touching sixty-four and a half thousand.
Its American funds lost one point seven nine billion last week. Lean: flat to lower. And issue one sixty-six's four leans fall due tomorrow. All four on course — bitcoin's only narrowly.
[chuckles] Narrowly is doing a lot of work there.
It is. Explanation, not advice. Now the sceptic, and I like this one. Kevin Lansing at the San Francisco Fed and Federico Nucera at the Bank of Italy.
With data, not a soundbite.

Their model says four economic variables explain most of the rise in valuations. It gives a fair Shiller ratio of thirty-five point eight. Friday's close had already reached thirty-six point four four.
[thoughtful] So the slide had mostly done its work before Huang came back.
On that evidence, yes. And page fifteen — Tuesday is earnings day.
The forecast for what S and P five hundred companies will earn over the next year — fifty-one per cent higher than in May twenty twenty-five.
Two hundred and seventy-seven dollars a share then. Four hundred and twenty now. And since the end of September, the index fell six point two per cent while expected earnings rose four point four.
So the whole fall was in what investors will pay. Not in the profits.

The forward price-to-earnings ratio went from twenty-two point nine to seventeen point one. And here's the unusual bit. FactSet's John Butters: "In a typical quarter, analysts usually reduce earnings estimates during the quarter."
And this quarter they raised them.
One point seven per cent. The cracks: the average beat is the smallest since late twenty twenty-two, and the seven big tech firms grew slower than the other four hundred and ninety-three.
And the cliff — sixteen point four per cent growth for twenty twenty-seven, three point six for its second quarter.
The call is held since issue one sixty-two: a real-rate shock. Nothing has tripped it.
Speaking of Nvidia — the Technology desk has the story behind the rally.
The board voted unanimously on Monday. And in the filing to the securities regulator, it said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government".
[gasps] They put that in writing.
In writing. And that, "based on that input", it's confident his return "poses no national security risk".
Six days earlier, the chair said they did not intend to reinstate him.
What changed was the White House. Trump told CNBC he intervened "directly and indirectly", and called Huang a "national treasure".
And Washington didn't split the way you'd expect.
No. Republican Don Bacon: "To me it's a failure of character." Senator John Cornyn: "No national security risk? Based on what?"
Though two of the loudest Republican critics are leaving Congress, which a Hacker News commenter was quick to point out.
Fair. The sceptic is Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: "It looks like a serious erosion of capitalism." And Huang goes before three House committees behind closed doors on the first of December.
The Home Lab has my favourite story of the week, honestly.
[amused] Go on.
Dragos, a security firm, sent about two million prompts to AI hosting companies, each laced with its own bait link and fake password. Then they watched where the bait turned up.
[wry] Like marked banknotes.

[excited] Exactly like marked banknotes. Three hosts had been breached since mid-July, and none of them knew. And a Chinese AI lab's scraper fetched secret links from more than half the prompts sent to its models.
Including the ones marked "zero data retention".
About two-thirds of those. HD Moore: "Zero Data Retention is supposed to mean something." OpenRouter dropped three providers and pulled a hundred and twenty-five endpoints.
And the sceptic: Dragos names nobody. Not the hosts, not the lab.
Which, as one commenter put it, is "trust us bro". The home-lab case makes itself. Run it yourself.
[deadpan] Subtle. The Kit, quickly. Google's Pixel Tag is on sale here at forty-four ninety-nine.
A coin-sized tracker, Android only. Engadget gave it eight point three. Nine to Five Google called it "the gold standard" for Android.
No keyring hole, though.
[laughs] No hole! You buy a holder. And the network is "hit or miss", says the same reviewer.
And the Atelier is hand-built bicycle wheels.
Which I love, because it's three bought parts and one skill. The hub, the spokes, the rim — and the person who tightens each spoke a quarter-turn at a time.
Chris King in Portland warrants its hubs for the original owner's lifetime. The R forty-five rear is five hundred and eighty US dollars.
And for us in Singapore, the nipples. The little nuts holding the spokes. Wheel Fanatyk says brass ones in the tropics "turn gray, then black, and crumble like stale cookies".
Builders here charge a hundred and twenty to a hundred and forty dollars to lace a pair. And the sceptic, Jobst Brandt: a machine-built wheel is fine "if the time is taken that the machine did not".
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single day.
Every single day. And today it's cryptic crosswords, which I think you secretly do.
[deadpan] I do them openly. On the train. With a pen.
[laughs] Of course with a pen. So for anyone who doesn't — every clue hides two routes to one answer. A plain definition at one end, and wordplay that builds the same word from parts.
Alan Connor's book is named after the classic. "Two girls, one on each knee," seven letters.
Pat, plus Ella. Patella. The kneecap.
[wry] It's a good one. It's annoying how good it is.
And the rule of fair play goes back to a setter called Afrit in nineteen forty-six — "You need not mean what you say, but you must say what you mean."
Now the news. On the tenth of October, the Times Crossword Championship in London. A hundred and thirteen qualifiers.
And a twenty-nine-year-old maths researcher from Helsinki, Liam Hughes, won it. Ten minutes five seconds, no mistakes. Youngest champion ever.
Mark Goodliffe, who has won it fourteen times, came fifth with one error.
[excited] But — running alongside them, with permission, outside the standings — a machine. Darmok, built by Professor Siddhartha Chatterjee at the University of Texas at Austin.
Six minutes fifty-two for the final. Every clue right, in every round.
Three minutes thirteen faster than the best human in the room.
The clue that sank three of the finalists was "Wolf trap missing its lowest crosspiece," five letters.
Snare — take the bottom stroke off the E, and it's an F. Snarf.
[sighs] Which is exactly the kind of clue I'd have stared at for ten minutes.
And the runner-up, Matthew Marcus, wrote: "I, for one, welcome our new A I overlords."
[chuckles] Gracious. But there's a caveat in the paper itself. Darmok ran three frontier AI models at once and solved the three puzzles in parallel.
Which no human can do. One mind and a pencil, as Chatterjee put it.
Where do solvers gather?
The blogs. Fifteensquared — "Never knowingly undersolved" — and Times for the Times. Every morning someone explains every clue, and the comments fill with times and groans.
And the Quick Cryptic for beginners drew ninety-eight comments yesterday against sixty-two for the main puzzle. That's where the newcomers are.
The setters all have pen-names. John Halpern is Paul in the Guardian, Punk in the Independent, Dada in the Telegraph and Mudd in the FT.

[amused] A man of many hats. The gear is cheap. The Times puzzles are a pound for three months, then four ninety-nine a month. The Chambers Dictionary — the setters' bible — thirty-nine ninety-nine, and not revised since twenty fourteen.
And the grail? Commission your own puzzle. Boatman starts at four hundred and fifty pounds — about thirty clues, half on your theme, two months' notice.
And this week, Don Manley — Bradman — set his three hundred and thirty-sixth and last puzzle for the FT.
[warmly] And the Independent's cryptic died on the thirty-first of October and comes back in the i Paper on Saturday. At least until January.
The sceptic: a minority taste, "like cricket", heavy on British general knowledge.
[laughs] Which, honestly, is part of the charm.
Culture and the body. Theo, you've got a watch.
[warmly] I have a watch. Roger W. Smith, the British maker on the Isle of Man — George Daniels's only apprentice — unveiled the Series Seven at his firm's twenty-fifth anniversary.
A tourbillon with an annual calendar. Price on request.
And he expects to make one or two a year. The maker calls it "very much a reflective piece".
The sceptic is SJX, who says the tourbillon's construction is "underwhelming" — and that wind the time back past midnight and the date jumps forward.
[sighs] Even the grail has a quirk. And Christie's Hong Kong sells a Patek Celestial tomorrow evening, at twelve to twenty-four million Hong Kong dollars.
Screen and Sound. I Play Rocky — Peter Farrelly's film about Stallone fighting to make Rocky — went wide and took nine point three million dollars, second place.
Ninety per cent with critics on Rotten Tomatoes, ninety-eight with audiences. Mick LaSalle says it's "every bit as good as Rocky".
And the Boston Globe's Odie Henderson calls it "an empty film" that "still loses the fight".
[laughs] Brutal. Sunrise on the Reaping, meanwhile, closed its opening weekend at a hundred and nineteen point three million.
The Family Desk, and this one's serious. JAMA Pediatrics, published yesterday: ten thousand and forty-eight pupils in southern China, followed for three years.
Short-video apps. And the key thing is it separates how long a child watches from whether the watching is compulsive.
Each extra year in the heavy-and-compulsive group raised the risk of a suicide attempt by sixty-three per cent.
[thoughtful] But the hopeful bit — the children who moved out of that pattern stopped accumulating the self-harm risk.
And the sceptic, Nick Ballou at Imperial College: low-mood teenagers may over-report their use, and addiction questionnaires contain low-mood items. It's observational. Not medical advice.
And then page thirteen — which, if you have a Primary Six child, is today.
PSLE results come out at eleven this morning. The Secondary One portal opens at eleven thirty and shuts at four thirty on Monday the thirtieth.
[exhales] Six days. To turn a number into a school.
The ministry's own advice, which people skip: cut-offs "can fluctuate", plus or minus one is typical, two or three possible. Put two or three schools with easier cut-offs on the list.
And how to react at eleven o'clock. Haimovitz and Dweck at Stanford found children pick up their parents' attitude to failure.
With a sceptic — a big meta-analysis that found mindset effects "weak".
[warmly] So it's not a lever. It's just a kindness. Ask what they learned.
Fitness. A Nature Medicine trial from the University of Western Australia — a hundred and twenty adults aged fifty to seventy, all on tirzepatide for forty weeks.
Half of them lifted weights three times a week. Both groups lost the same weight — about twenty-two and a half kilos.
But the lifters lost a kilo less lean tissue. And they got stronger. Lat pulldown up eight and a half kilos, against a fall of four and a half on the drug alone.
The try-this: three full-body sessions a week, a squat, a pull and a push, a month on technique first.
Caveats: no arm that trained without the drug, nobody blinded, and Lilly supplied the drug. Not medical advice.
The Diary. The pick is Disney On Ice — Let's Dance — at the Indoor Stadium, thirteenth to twenty-first of March.
The presale closes at eleven fifty-nine tonight. General sale opens at ten tomorrow.
[excited] And in Tokyo, a Final Fantasy fortieth-anniversary exhibition at the Tokyo National Museum, from the eighth of January. Child tickets eleven hundred yen. Timed entry, advance only.
And on The Table, British Hainan has reopened in a Tiong Bahru coffeeshop. Pork chop, seventeen ninety. One review so far, so — too new to call.
Which brings us to the Long Read.
[thoughtful] On the fifth of November, a Tokyo publisher named its thirty nominees for Japan's word of the year. Seventh on the list was gengoka.
[warmly] Putting it into words.
Language, plus "-isation". The act of turning a feeling into sentences someone else can follow.
[thoughtful] And it matters because Japan prized the opposite. Reading the air. Sensing what someone means without being told.
A dictionary editor counted it in four national papers — a handful to fifty uses a year in the twenty-tens, more than two hundred a year in the twenty-twenties.
And the government's own language survey — in two thousand and eight, thirty-eight per cent valued putting things into words. By twenty sixteen, half.
The coach Takuro Yamaguchi has the line of the essay. "AI does not read the room."
[warmly] Which is lovely. And his deeper point — "the culture of sensing has not declined; what has been lost are the conditions that made sensing possible."
Jobs for life. One office. A few television channels. All going.
In two thousand and seven, the buzzword was "KY" — can't read the air — an insult for the person who missed the mood. This year the buzzword praises the person who spells it out.
The sceptic: the loudest advocates are selling books, and most Japanese still avoid confrontation. It could be a fashion.
[thoughtful] And a student on X put the cost better than anyone. "The moment you put it into words, it shifts."
Our call: gengoka makes the top ten on the first of December, but doesn't win. We'll print it either way.
[warmly] And somewhere in Singapore, a country of polite indirection, someone is reading this and recognising it.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-five pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
